title: Datamosh
description: Nine seconds of a rail journey in two shots, played through a video codec that runs live: an encoder and a decoder rebuilding every frame from the one before, block by block along real motion vectors, with residuals through an 8x8 DCT and an I-frame every three seconds and on the cut. Six seconds out of a summer train window, a lateral pan that runs from a low tree line into a stand of oaks, then a hard cut to three seconds of winter track rushing at the camera out of a vanishing point. The decoder tunes in mid-stream, so the picture first assembles out of the paper from nothing but what moves. Press and drag and the codec breaks only under your hand: the macroblocks you paint lose the next I-frame, and every intra block in them is turned into an inter block along its neighbours' vectors, the way a datamosher strips them, while the rest of the picture decodes true. Paint over the cut and the winter shot arrives everywhere but your stroke, where the decoder repeats the first winter P-frame over and over, every partition along its own vector, finding nothing of its own to move and pushing the summer picture instead: the oak branches and the sky between them by the vanishing point are dragged out of it, further every frame, in long stepped radial streaks on the macroblock grid that run from intact leaves out into strip, while at the ends of the strips, which tear out along their rays to different lengths, the winter picture is torn into the strips and the strips out across it. Keep holding and the tear spreads downstream along the motion, blooming out over seconds until it has taken most of the ground, torn into a winter frame that stays intact around it. Dragging also runs the clip faster under your hand. Let go and the tear fades from its edges, drifts, and a column of intra blocks sweeps it clean.
intent: Datamoshing as the actual codec process rather than a glitch shader, after Takeshi Murata's Monster Movie (2005, https://www.eai.org/titles/monster-movie) and Rosa Menkman's A Vernacular of File Formats (2010, https://li-ma.nl/article/vernacular-of-file-formats-summary), and herb's generative references 2 (a street photo whose region is smeared into strips while the rest stays intact) and 3 (real analog artefacts from a real signal model). Motion vectors are baked offline by block matching on the shipped VP9 frames (tools/depth/bakes/datamosh/mv.py: 16x16 macroblocks, 8x8 partitions where the SAD saving beats a split cost, hierarchical full search to +-56 px, H.264-style rate term toward the neighbours' median vector, half-pel refinement, the zero vector wherever standing still predicts about as well (so featureless overcast does not carry a vector found once in its noise for the rest of the shot), intra where the best prediction is worse than DC), packed as per-MB modes plus median-predicted vector differences. Live in WebGL2 an encoder and a decoder run frame by frame: H.264 six-tap half-pel motion compensation, residual against the encoder's own reconstruction through a separable 8x8 DCT with a dead-zone quantiser (QP 30), closed loop, I-frames every 90 frames and wherever the stream carries a keyframe. The clip is two shots with a hard cut at frame 180, on an I-frame, so the I-frame a hold drops is a real scene change: the second shot (a forward run down a single track, every vector radial out of the vanishing point) moves the first shot's pixels, the reference/motion mismatch that makes a P-frame bloom. The seam back to the start is the same cut the other way: the lateral pan drags the winter picture sideways. The decoder joins between I-frames from blank paper. The hand starves it one macroblock at a time (herb's ref 2: the smear bounded by an untouched photo): a per-macroblock mask painted by a soft brush about five blocks across along the pointer path while held, fading with a 1.6 s time constant after release, and read along the rays out of the vanishing point (the median of the clip's fitted zoom centres) rather than block by block: one ray per 8 px of frame edge, each with its own random reach (two octaves of value noise round the edge plus a little of its own, so neighbouring rays that share a macroblock near the centre end together), and a block is starved only where the brush level times its ray's reach exceeds its distance along the ray from the stroke's inner edge, normalised so the frame edge is 1; a ray that has ended stays fed until it leaves the stroke, every block upstream of a starved one is starved back to the stroke's inner edge (a diagonal step also takes the block between, so a strip never breaks into corner-touching squares), and a block that has lost its I-frame stays torn while the hand holds, so no block in a ray decodes true while the ray is moshed past it and the tear's boundary is the ends of radial strips of different lengths (ref 2's strip ends), not a stepped outline (an earlier version gave every block its own random threshold, which left a hard 16 px staircase and confetti: true-picture squares inside the tear and stray mosh squares outside it). A starved block strips its intra blocks the way ffglitch and Murata strip them: each intra macroblock in a P-frame becomes an inter one along the median of its neighbours' vectors (filled inward over clusters, zero where nothing is near); until the next I-frame its P-frames otherwise arrive whole, residual and all, so the picture under the hand stays itself up to the I-frame it loses (an earlier version starved the residual from the first touch, and two seconds of the lateral pan without it ground the summer picture into a uniform 8x8 mottle before the cut ever came). From the dropped I-frame on it gets no residual, is predicted from the moshed picture, and every held block is copied in whole pels with no interpolation (fractional vectors stepped by error diffusion per 8x8 partition, so a partition always steps the same way), so the photo's grain and the block edges stay sharp through hundreds of frames and the smear moves in hard stepped strips instead of the six-tap filter low-passing it into airbrush, so the bloom is one continuous flow-driven smear rather than scattered squares of the true picture; once a starved block has missed an I-frame it stops taking new vectors and duplicates one P-frame, the classic datamosh: the first P-frame after the dropped I-frame, kept whole (a block the tear reaches later repeats the same frame), every 8x8 partition with its own vector at full magnitude, so the field keeps its radial divergence (an earlier version averaged four P-frames and took a 3x3 median, which made neighbouring partitions step alike and compounded the picture into mottle); only the bake's zero vectors, which it writes wherever standing still predicts about as well, are read the way H.264 reads P_Skip, along the median of the partitions around them, so they do not sit as still squares in the rays. When the frame is a zoom (a least-squares fit of v = -c (p - centre) with c over 0.01 per px: the forward run, not the summer pan) each vector is also weighted by the square of its partition's distance from the fitted centre over 500 px, at most 1.3, so what lies near the centre stays itself and further out each partition reads further in than the one inside it: frozen and applied again to its own moshed picture on every frame of the hold, the oak branches and the sky between them are copied out along their rays, one partition further each frame, into long stepped radial streaks that grade from intact picture into strip (ref 2). One macroblock past the end of each starved ray the edge repeats the same P-frame from the moshed picture but still takes the I-frame, so the winter picture is dragged into the strips from it and the strips out across it, and the tear has no cut-out edge. While the hand holds, the starved mask itself is advected downstream along the vectors (each fed block takes on the level of the block its vector reads from, one macroblock upstream, at a rate of 0.3 per 16 px of vector per frame, at most 0.5), so the tear blooms outward with the motion and not at all where the picture stands still: a 4 s hold over the cut takes about 40% of the frame, a 0.6 s one a fifth; every other block is fed and decodes the true frame. Vectors that reach past the frame edge are read mirrored back in rather than edge-extended, so a starved block at the border does not comb into one-pixel streaks. A block fed again after being starved decodes honestly from its damaged reference, so the mosh drifts along the true vectors until an intra block, an I-frame or the intra refresh that sweeps the macroblock columns after a release cleans it. Stills paint a fixed stroke over the first 0.3 s of their hold, a V down the lower third with its apex on the winter shot's vanishing point and both arms along its radial vectors, where they run longest; at the cut the oak stand fills that band, so the vectors drag leaves and the sky between them, not flat blue, into the strips (a stroke that stops short of the vanishing point is refilled with the true winter picture from behind within a few frames, since everything outside it moves outward): ?t=8&hold=4 (the hero) holds it across the cut, ?t=6.3&hold=0.6 a moment after it; ?t=seconds stops the stream there, ?hold=seconds of hold before it, ?release=seconds before it lets go (the refresh mid-sweep), ?join=1 shows the opening, ?qp= sets the quantiser.

sources.author: ChristianBodhi
sources.note: 3840x2160, 30 fps, 27.2 s, out of a train window; location not given. Seconds 15.35-21.35 used (shot A), the lower half of the frame (1920x1080 from 960,1080) so the tree line and the oaks that run in at the end fill the picture below the sky, scaled to 1280x720 (Lanczos). Joined by a hard cut to shot B (below), then two-pass VP9 at 5 Mb/s with no alt-ref (clip.webm, 270 frames; libvpx keyframes at 0 and on the cut); motion vectors and modes baked from those decoded frames by tools/depth/bakes/datamosh/mv.py with a +-56 px search both ways (clip.mv, gzip).

sources.author: Bonaparcik
sources.note: 2048x922 as downloaded (2400x1080 original), 30 fps, 18 s, single track through pine forest in early winter, filmed out of the back of a train. Seconds 14.9-17.9 used (shot B, frames 180-269; source frames 447-536): the last stretch, out past the pines into open verge, where the shutter freezes the ballast, the snow and the bare birches (about twice the edge energy of the motion-blurred seconds 3-6 used before), so the strips tear against a sharp photo; cropped to 16:9 past the window pillar, scaled to 1280x720 (Lanczos) and run backwards, so the line comes at the camera.
